=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Patient: male | Age: None
Primary Diagnosis: Pulmonary tuberculosis (sensitive to isoniazid and rifampin)

  Secondary: Lung collapse
  Secondary: Pleural effusion (fluid in the chest cavity)
  Secondary: Right pneumonectomy (removal of right lung)
  Secondary: Surgical wound infection
  Secondary: Multidrug‑resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection
  Secondary: Hypovolemic shock (low blood volume)
  Secondary: Cardiopulmonary arrest (heart stopped)
  Secondary: Bleeding in tuberculous cavities
Symptoms at admission: persistent dry cough for 4 weeks; night sweats; fever (not measured); dyspnea (shortness of breath); sudden right chest pain radiating to right neck; progressive worsening of breathing; weight loss of about 8 kg
Anomalies/Findings:
  [NORMAL] Heart rate = 85 beats per minute (normal: 60-100 bpm)
  [NORMAL] Oxygen saturation = 98% (normal: 95-100%)
  [BORDERLINE] Procalcitonin = 0.09 ng/mL (normal: <0.05 ng/mL)
  [ABNORMAL] Acid‑fast bacilli count = 10 to 99 per 100 fields (normal: 0 per 100 fields)
  [CRITICAL] Hypovolemic shock
  [CRITICAL] Cardiopulmonary arrest
  [ABNORMAL] Spontaneous pneumothorax
  [ABNORMAL] Lung collapse
  [ABNORMAL] Pleural effusion
  [ABNORMAL] Surgical wound infection
  [ABNORMAL] Multidrug‑resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection
  [ABNORMAL] Bleeding in tuberculous cavities = significant oozing
Procedures performed:
  • Right chest drainage on 02/03/2020
  • Pleurostomy on 03/03/2020
  • Pleurostomy closure
  • Heimlich valve insertion on 03/10/2020
  • Removal of Heimlich valve on 03/27/2020
  • New pleurotomy on 03/31/2020
  • Exploratory thoracotomy on 04/07/2020
  • Packing of cavity with compresses on 04/07/2020
  • Right pneumonectomy by lateral thoracotomy on 04/11/2020
  • Tracheostomy on 04/11/2020
  • Chest drain removal on 06/06/2020
  • Tracheostomy removal on 06/06/2020
Medications:
  • Vancomycin — kills bacteria that are hard to treat
  • Meropenem — kills a wide range of bacteria
  • Amikacin — kills bacteria that are resistant to other drugs
  • Oral iron replacement — helps make healthy blood cells
Warning signs to mention:
  ⚠ Sudden chest pain or worsening breathing
  ⚠ Fever or chills
  ⚠ Bleeding or blood in sputum
  ⚠ Sudden collapse or fainting
  ⚠ Shortness of breath that gets worse
  ⚠ Any signs of infection at the surgical wound

Follow-up appointment: Follow‑up at [organization] (date not specified)
Ongoing treatment: Oral iron replacement
Ongoing treatment: Antibiotic therapy stopped after 02/04
Hospital stay duration: 3 months 6 days 7 hours
Outcome: alive
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
You have pulmonary tuberculosis (a lung infection caused by TB germs) that is sensitive to isoniazid and rifampin (the medicines that can kill these germs). In addition, you have several other problems caused by the TB: a spontaneous pneumothorax (air that has entered the space around the right lung), lung collapse (the right lung has fallen down), pleural effusion (fluid that has collected in the chest cavity), a right pneumonectomy (surgical removal of the whole right lung), a surgical wound infection (infection where the chest was cut), a multidrug‑resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection (a very tough bacteria that does not respond to many antibiotics), hypovolemic shock (very low blood volume because of bleeding), cardiopulmonary arrest (your heart stopped for a short time), and bleeding in tuberculous cavities (significant oozing from the infected areas in the lung).

When you came to the hospital you had a dry cough that had lasted for four weeks, night sweats, a fever that you did not measure, shortness of breath (dyspnea), a sudden sharp pain in the right side of the chest that spread to the right side of the neck, and the breathing got worse step by step. You also lost about eight kilograms (about 17‑18 pounds) in the last month. You did not cough up blood or any sputum.

Your heart was beating at 85 beats per minute; the normal range is 60‑100, so this was normal. Your oxygen saturation was 98 %; the normal range is 95‑100, also normal. The procalcitonin level was 0.09 ng/mL; the normal is less than 0.05, so this was a little higher than normal (borderline). The acid‑fast bacilli count in your sputum was 10‑99 per 100 fields; normally it should be zero, so this was abnormal and showed TB bacteria present. You also had critical problems of hypovolemic shock and cardiopulmonary arrest, and abnormal findings of spontaneous pneumothorax, lung collapse, pleural effusion, surgical wound infection, multidrug‑resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection, and bleeding in tuberculous cavities (significant oozing).

Several procedures were done to treat these problems. On 02/03/2020 a right chest drainage (a tube placed to remove air or fluid from the chest) was performed. On 03/03/2020 a pleurostomy (a surgical opening made in the chest wall to let air and fluid out) was done, and later the pleurostomy was closed. On 03/10/2020 a Heimlich valve (a one‑way valve that lets air escape from the chest) was inserted, and on 03/27/2020 that valve was removed while keeping the drain open for the pleurostomy. On 03/31/2020 a new pleurotomy (another opening in the chest) was created. Because of heavy bleeding from the TB cavities, an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (opening the chest to look inside) was performed on 04/07/2020, and the bleeding cavity was packed with compresses (gauze pieces) on the same day. On 04/11/2020 a right pneumonectomy by lateral thoracotomy (removal of the whole right lung through a side opening in the chest) was carried out, and at the same time a tracheostomy (a hole made in the windpipe to help breathing) was done. The chest drain and the tracheostomy tube were both taken out on 06/06/2020.

For the tough bacterial infection you were given vancomycin (a medicine that kills bacteria that are hard to treat), meropenem (a medicine that kills a wide range of bacteria), and amikacin (a medicine that kills bacteria that are resistant to other drugs). You also received oral iron replacement (iron tablets that help your body make healthy blood cells). The antibiotic therapy was stopped after 02/04 because you improved clinically and your procalcitonin level fell to 0.09 ng/mL.

You were warned to call the hospital immediately if you notice any of the following warning signs: sudden chest pain or worsening breathing, fever or chills, bleeding or blood in the sputum, sudden collapse or fainting, shortness of breath that gets worse, or any signs of infection at the surgical wound (such as redness, swelling, or pus).

You need to follow up with the thoracic surgery team (date not given) and also with [organization] (date not given). You should continue taking oral iron replacement as prescribed. The antibiotic medicines have already been stopped after 02/04.

You were admitted on 03/02/2020 and discharged on 09/05/2020, staying in the hospital for three months, six days, and seven hours. You are alive and in good general condition at the time of discharge.
